The bill would restore standard drug enforcement and diversion programs in the Australian Capital Territory.
It would cancel the 2022 ACT law that changed how small amounts of drugs are treated, so old offence rules and penalties apply again.
The bill would start the day after it receives Royal Assent and would not affect anything done before that date.
The bill would stop the Drugs of Dependence (Personal Use) Amendment Act 2022 (ACT) from having any effect.
It would keep the existing offence provisions from the Drugs of Dependence Act 1989 (ACT), without different treatment for small quantities of drugs.
The bill would prevent the use of simple drug offence notices for substances listed in tables 6.1 and 6.2 of the Drugs of Dependence Regulation 2009 (ACT).
ACT families, police, pharmacists and the general community are affected.

This bill would make more Indigenous students eligible for government-funded university places.
It would remove the rule that students must pass half their subjects to keep their funded place and require universities to have a policy to help students succeed.
The government would fund all Indigenous students in bachelor degrees at Table A providers with no cap on numbers, except for medicine courses.
Expands eligibility for Commonwealth supported places to all First Nations students, including those in metropolitan areas.
Removes the 50 per cent pass requirement for Commonwealth supported places and FEE-HELP assistance.
Requires higher education providers to have and comply with a student support policy.
First Nations students and higher education providers listed as Table A providers.

This bill is part of a package that would create a $10 billion fund to boost social and affordable housing, and set up an independent advisory body on housing policy.
The fund would be managed by the Future Fund Board, with its earnings spent on housing for Indigenous communities, women, children, veterans, and other groups in need.
The bill would start on a day fixed by Proclamation, or six months after it receives Royal Assent, whichever comes first.
The bill would establish the Housing Australia Future Fund to provide a dedicated funding source for social and affordable housing.
The bill would create the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council as an independent body to advise the government on housing supply and affordability.
The bill would allocate $330 million to address acute housing needs over the fund's first five years.
The explanatory memorandum says the bill would affect people needing social or affordable housing, Indigenous communities, women, children, veterans, and the Future Fund Board.

The majority voted in favour of *disagreeing* with a second reading amendment introduced by Griffith MP [Max Chandler-Mather](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/griffith/max_chandler-mather) (Greens), which means it failed. The Selection of Bills Committee presented its first report of 2023, referring multiple bills to committees for inquiry, including the Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023 and related housing bills to the Economics Legislation Committee with a reporting date of 22 March. Senator McKim moved an unsuccessful amendment to extend that reporting date to 22 April, arguing the government's housing response is inadequate and a longer inquiry is needed to hear from renters and housing sector stakeholders.

The motion to change committee memberships was agreed, with Senator Faruqi replacing McKim on the Economics Legislation Committee for the Housing Australia Future Fund Bill inquiry, and McKim replacing Shoebridge on the Legal and Constitutional Affairs Committee for the Migration Amendment (Evacuation to Safety) Bill inquiry. Senators Bilyk, Brockman, Payne, Shoebridge, Sterle and White were appointed to the National Anti-Corruption Commission Joint Statutory Committee.

The speaker argued that the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation Bill 2022 and the Housing Australia Future Fund Bill 2023 are urgent election commitments that will rebuild manufacturing, create jobs, reduce imports, and lower social costs, and criticised opposition to the bills as politically and economically senseless.
